newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: First Dutch swine fever case outside infected area.
newsitem.headline: First Dutch swine fever case outside infected area.

text.p: The Dutch farm ministry said on Friday it had detected another case of swine fever, the first to be discovered outside a previously designated infected area, in which all livestock transport has been banned.
"The new case is at a farm just outside the old area and this will be extended accordingly," a spokesman told Reuters.

There are now 181 farms, where the highly contagious disease has been detected, some three months after the first case came to light. All are in the south of the Netherlands, where most of the country's pigs 14 million are reared.
Nearly 50 new cases have been discovered this month alone.
"There will be no additional measures taken aside from extending the area," the ministry spokesman added.

The ministry said some 1.6 million pigs had so far been destroyed in a bid to control the outbreak, which has led to many countries banning Dutch imports of live pigs, costing the country millions of guilders in lost export revenue.

In addition, the government has won European Union permission to kill some 500,000 recently piglets born within the boundaries of the infected area. All piglets aged between three and 17 days will be killed, and mostly funded by the EU.
In livestock markets throughout the Netherlands, wholesale prices of live pigs have soared to all-time highs, and this is now feeding through to higher prices on supermarket shelves.

Because the Netherlands is leading exporter, earning around five billion guilders from the trade last year, there has been a knock-on effect on pork prices throughout Europe, accentuated by other cases of swine fever in other countries.
In Spain, where there has also been a swine fever outbreak, pork prices are up some 40 percent this year.

In another major European exporter, Denmark, supplies have re-directed from other European countries to Japan, whose traditional supplier Taiwan has cut back its own exports due to an outbreak of foot-and-mouth hog disease.
